models.author: Shreyash Gade
models.description:
# 🚀 MiniLM Sentence Transformer

This model is based on **all-MiniLM-L6-v2** from Sentence Transformers and is designed to generate high-quality sentence embeddings.

---

## 🔍 Use Cases

- Semantic Similarity
- Resume Matching
- Document Search
- Chatbot Understanding
- Clustering & Recommendation Systems

---

## ⚡ Features

- Lightweight & Fast
- Works on CPU and GPU
- Produces 384-dimensional embeddings
- Suitable for real-time applications

---

## 💻 Example Usage

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

model = SentenceTransformer("/kaggle/input/minilm-sentence-transformer")

sentences = ["I love AI", "Artificial Intelligence is amazing"]
embeddings = model.encode(sentences)

similarity = cosine_similarity([embeddings[0]], embeddings[1:])
print(similarity)

instances.overview:

Optimized for fast inference on CPU and GPU.
instances.usage:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

# Load model
model = SentenceTransformer("/kaggle/input/minilm-sentence-transformer")

# Example sentences
sentences = ["I love AI", "Artificial Intelligence is amazing"]

# Generate embeddings
embeddings = model.encode(sentences)

# Compute similarity
similarity = cosine_similarity([embeddings[0]], embeddings[1:])
print("Similarity Score:", similarity)

models.description:
Description:

A curated collection of highly optimized, pre-trained PyTorch weights designed specifically for the Stanford RNA 3D Folding Part 2 competition.

Predicting the complex, thermodynamic ensembles of ribonucleic acid requires massive computational capacity and sophisticated spatial reasoning. This repository contains the foundational architectural weights—including highly tuned variants of Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (EGNNs) and spatial transformers—necessary to accurately model these deep topological geometries.

Engineered strictly for seamless integration into offline, internet-disabled Kaggle inference pipelines, these models have been calibrated to support rigorous structural ensembling. They provide the latent geometric diversity required to successfully execute Best-of-5 conformational generation without catastrophic coordinate degradation.

Key Features:


Native PyTorch .pt format for immediate Dataloader integration.

Optimized for sub-linear inference scaling under strict 8-hour GPU runtime limits.

Architectures specifically tuned to preserve Euclidean (E(3)) and Special Euclidean (SE(3)) physical symmetries.
models.subtitle: Optimized PyTorch spatial architectures for advanced RNA tertiary structure prediction and offline inference.

| Model Identity | Model name | Rock Segmentation Model (YOLOv26-seg family) |
| Model Identity | Version(s) | segment_L_v1, segment_L_v2, segment_M, segment_S |
| Model Identity | Task | Instance segmentation of rocks in rover camera imagery |
| Model Identity | Status | Experimental deployment-ready for assisted perception; not safety-certified |
| Architecture | Base architecture | Ultralytics YOLO segmentation architecture |
| Architecture | Initialization | Fine-tuned from pretrained segmentation weights (not trained from scratch) |
| Architecture | Output types | Per-instance masks, bounding boxes, confidence scores, class labels |
| Architecture | Typical inference size | 640 to 960 square input size (deployment commonly uses 960 where compute allows) |
| Usage | Primary use | Real-time obstacle perception support, offline image/video analysis, edge deployment on Jetson |
| Usage | Input shape | Runtime image/frame: H x W x 3 (uint8), internally resized to batch tensor B x 3 x imgsz x imgsz |
| Usage | Output shape | Boxes: N x 4, Scores: N, Classes: N, Masks: N x Hm x Wm |
| Usage | Example thresholds | Segmentation confidence threshold typically 0.40 or higher |
| Usage | Known preventable failures | Missed small/far rocks at low resolution; false positives in clutter; domain-shift failures under unseen lighting/terrain |
| Usage | Failure mitigations | Increase input size, tune confidence, add hard negatives, collect target-domain data, retrain/fine-tune periodically |
| System Context | Standalone or system | Part of a larger perception stack (camera capture, inference runtime, downstream rover logic) |
| System Context | Input requirements | RGB camera/image/video stream, trained weights, configured runtime device (GPU/CPU) |
| System Context | Downstream dependencies | Ultralytics runtime for PT inference; ONNX/TensorRT path for optimized edge deployment; OpenCV for capture/visualization |
| Implementation | Training software | Python, PyTorch, Ultralytics YOLO |
| Implementation | Deployment software | Ultralytics, OpenCV, ONNX export tools, TensorRT tooling on Jetson |
| Implementation | Training hardware | CUDA-capable GPU used; exact chip count not formally logged |
| Implementation | Inference hardware | Desktop GPU and Jetson-class edge GPU supported; CPU fallback available |
| Implementation | Training time/compute | Example run profile includes up to 250 epochs at imgsz 640; total FLOPs/energy not formally reported |
| Model Stats | Model size/params | Exact parameter counts and layer counts not yet published in project documentation |
| Model Stats | Latency | Hardware- and backend-dependent; medium variant generally best speed/quality balance |
| Model Stats | Optimization | ONNX export and TensorRT engine build supported for edge acceleration |
| Model Stats | Pruning/quantization | No formal pruning or quantization report in current model documentation |
| Privacy/Security | Differential privacy | Not applied/documented |
| Data Overview | Data sources | Rock detection and rock segmentation datasets from project Kaggle releases |
| Data Overview | Collection summary | Labeled field imagery for rock scenes; includes challenging examples and reported false negatives |
| Data Overview | Preprocessing | YOLO-format dataset configuration, resizing/augmentation handled by training pipeline |
| Data Overview | Split strategy | Train/validation/test directories used |
| Data Overview | Demographic groups | No human demographic target; relevant subgroup axes are environmental (distance, lighting, terrain, viewpoint) |
| Evaluation | Current evidence | Primarily qualitative and engineering validation; formal benchmark table still pending |
| Evaluation | Relative model observations | segment_L_v1 reported strongest quality; segment_M reported best practical speed/load tradeoff |
| Evaluation | Subgroup evaluation | Not yet fully completed; recommended slices: near/far, day/night, dry/wet terrain, high/low texture |
| Fairness | Fairness definition (task-appropriate) | Performance consistency across environmental subgroups rather than human demographic parity |
| Fairness | Suggested metrics | Per-subgroup mask mAP, false-negative rate by distance bucket, confidence calibration by lighting condition |
| Limitations | Sensitive use cases | High-risk autonomous navigation without independent safety layer |
| Limitations | Usage constraints | Do not use as sole safety mechanism; require fallback logic, conservative controls, and operator override |
| Ethics | Risks identified | Over-trust risk in unseen environments; missed hazards under domain shift |
| Ethics | Mitigations | Human-in-the-loop safeguards, conservative deployment thresholds, ongoing data refresh and re-evaluation |
| Governance | Recommended release artifacts | Add quantitative benchmark table, latency by hardware/backend, and subgroup performance report before broader deployment |

instances.usage:
## Example Usage

Use these pretrained weights for rock detection and segmentation in images, videos, or live camera feeds.

### 1) Install dependencies

```bash
pip install -q ultralytics opencv-python
```

### 2) Python inference example (segmentation + detection)

```python
from ultralytics import YOLO
import cv2

# Load models
seg_model = YOLO("segment_L_v2.pt")   # or segment_L_v1.pt / segment_M.pt
det_model = YOLO("detection.pt")

# Read input image
image = cv2.imread("/kaggle/input/your-dataset/sample.jpg")

# Segmentation inference
seg_results = seg_model.predict(
    source=image,
    imgsz=960,
    conf=0.40,      # recommended minimum for segmentation visualization
    device=0,       # use "cpu" if GPU is not available
    verbose=False
)

# Detection inference
det_results = det_model.predict(
    source=image,
    imgsz=640,
    conf=0.25,
    device=0,
    verbose=False
)

# Save annotated outputs
seg_annotated = seg_results[0].plot()
det_annotated = det_results[0].plot()
cv2.imwrite("segmentation_result.jpg", seg_annotated)
cv2.imwrite("detection_result.jpg", det_annotated)

print("Segmentation masks:", seg_results[0].masks is not None)
print("Detections:", 0 if det_results[0].boxes is None else len(det_results[0].boxes))
```

### 3) CLI quick run

```bash
# Segmentation
python -m ultralytics predict model=segment_L_v2.pt source=/kaggle/input/your-dataset/sample.jpg imgsz=960 conf=0.40 device=0

# Detection
python -m ultralytics predict model=detection.pt source=/kaggle/input/your-dataset/sample.jpg imgsz=640 conf=0.25 device=0
```

### Notes for best results
- Use higher image size (for example 960) to improve small/far rock segmentation.
- If FPS is low or memory is limited, reduce image size to 640.
- For unseen terrain/lighting, fine-tune on target-domain data for better robustness.
